content_voiceover: This slide walks through the NCCN treatment algorithm for ATLL, stratified by clinical subtype, plus the prognostic scoring systems used to risk-stratify patients. For smoldering ATLL, asymptomatic patients can simply be observed or enrolled in a clinical trial, while symptomatic patients with skin lesions get skin-directed therapy or zidovudine plus interferon. Chronic ATLL is further split by risk: low and intermediate risk patients, defined by soluble IL-2 receptor level, can receive zidovudine and interferon, while high-risk chronic disease, with elevated LDH, low albumin, or very high soluble IL-2 receptor, gets escalated to systemic combination therapy. Acute and lymphoma subtypes are the aggressive ones, treated upfront with systemic therapy or zidovudine plus interferon, with response assessed after two cycles; responders continue treatment or move to allogeneic transplant, while non-responders switch to second-line therapy. For prognosis, the ATL-PI applies to acute and lymphoma subtypes, using stage, ECOG performance status, age over seventy, low albumin, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor to define low, intermediate, and high risk groups. A modified index for younger aggressive ATLL adds CRP and calcium levels. The overarching message is that risk stratification, both by clinical subtype and by these prognostic indices, directly drives the decision between watchful waiting, antiviral therapy, and intensive combination chemotherapy with transplant consideration.
keypoints: Smoldering: observation, or skin-directed therapy/zidovudine+interferon if symptomatic
Chronic: zidovudine+interferon; high-risk chronic escalates to systemic therapy
Acute/lymphoma: upfront systemic therapy, response-adapted, consider allo-HCT if responding
ATL-PI (acute/lymphoma): stage, ECOG, age >70, low albumin, high sIL-2R
Modified PI (age <70): swaps in CRP and calcium level
